Sotheby’s Georgia and WHO deliver 2,000 rabies immunoglobulin vials to Ukraine Saturday, 18 July 2026, 07:14 A fresh shipment of 2,000 rabies immunoglobulin vials arrived for urgent regional distribution. Health officials say the supply will support post-exposure treatment for high-risk patients. As reported by the online media Ukrinform. Two thousand vials of rabies immunoglobulin have arrived in Ukraine, which will be distributed among the regions in the near future to ensure medical facilities that provide care to patients at risk of rabies infection. The Ministry of Health reported that the delivery was made possible thanks to the support of the Georgian government and the World Health Organization. This delivery was made possible thanks to the support of the Georgian government and the World Health Organization. The received rabies immunoglobulin will be promptly distributed among the regions so that medical facilities providing anti-rabies care have the necessary resources to treat patients according to medical indications. – Ihor Kuzin Context and actions for rabies prevention In the health system at the level of regional medical facilities, designated rabies care centers have been established: they are stocked with vaccines, the doctors at the centers provide medical care to patients who seek help after bites, scratches, or exposure to animals; they perform initial treatment; prescribe and administer courses of anti-rabies vaccinations as needed. Rabies is a particularly dangerous infectious disease that can be completely prevented with timely medical help and the implementation of post-exposure prophylaxis. The basis of rabies prevention is the rabies vaccine, which is used in the vast majority of cases after bites or contacts with potentially infected animals. Rabies immunoglobulin is not required for everyone after a bite or exposure to animals – only in cases of high risk of infection. In particular, with severe or multiple bites, bites to the head, neck, hands, or exposure of mucous membranes. The choice of prophylaxis scheme is determined solely by the physician based on an assessment of risk for each specific case: to prescribe only a course of rabies vaccination or, if necessary, to combine vaccination with administration of rabies immunoglobulin. According to the Ministry of Health, in May the regions received over 42,000 doses of the rabies vaccine. Cases of rabies infections are rising, in particular due to military actions in the country. This delivery underscores the importance of coordinating efforts in the health sector and supporting international partners in the fight against the virus. We recommend paying attention to: Over 260 people in Donetsk sought medical care for animal bites in Q1 2026; health authorities say vaccines and immunoglobulin were provided and urge continued vigilance against rabies. The Ministry of Health delivered 42,650 rabies vaccine doses to regional Centers for Disease Control; doses will be distributed to anti-rabies clinics to strengthen post-exposure prophylaxis. Ukraine’s health committee urges modernizing tobacco legislation to cover snus, e-cigarettes, and other nicotine products, aiming to curb youth targeting and strengthen public health protections. Australian land forces join Norway led Legio training in Poland to boost Ukrainian readiness Saturday, 18 July 2026, 06:45 Australian instructors embedded in the Kudu operation have joined Norway’s Legio training in Poland. The collaboration pushes tactics to the limit to expose weaknesses before combat. As reported by the online media Ukrinform. Representatives of the Australian Army’s Land Forces joined the training of Ukrainian defenders in Poland. According to official information from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s press service, this was confirmed on their page. The personnel of the Kudu training operation of the Australian Army have joined the Legio training operation under the leadership of the Norwegian Armed Forces Forsvaret in Poland to jointly conduct high-quality training of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, aimed at increasing the effectiveness of Ukrainian units on the battlefield – General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Within the training, Ukrainian and Australian instructors work side by side, creating highly realistic scenarios. A hallmark of this course is testing tactical plans to the brink of mistakes in a safe training environment. Such an approach allows early identification of weaknesses, a detailed analysis of unit actions, and rapid elimination of deficiencies even before entering real combat zones. In addition to practicing practical skills, the collaboration among allies aims to foster an unbreakable combat spirit and psychological resilience. The training helps Ukrainian defenders rapidly adapt to the changing conditions of modern confrontation, develop flexible tactical thinking, and step by step form a hardened warrior mindset today to confidently defeat the enemy tomorrow. Under the motto “adapt and win,” Australian soldiers together with multinational partners are doing everything possible to help Ukraine win the war on its own terms. As explained by the General Staff, military assistance from partners is implemented through several key initiatives. Kudu and Legio Initiative: Figures and Objectives Operation Kudu is a large-scale program of the Australian Defence Forces, within which Australian instructors train Ukrainian servicemen. Operation Legio, led by the Norwegian Armed Forces on Polish territory, focuses on providing in-depth and specialized training. The integration of the Australian Kudu contingent into the Norwegian Legio operation is an example of effective alliance coordination for high-quality training of Ukrainian forces in Europe, the General Staff summed up. The Legio initiative, launched in 2024 under Norway’s leadership, brought together nine Nordic and Baltic countries: Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, and Sweden. The initiative provides: training of Ukrainian military personnel by partner-country instructors; equipping various Ukrainian units with weapons in amounts equivalent to brigade sizes, in accordance with NATO standards; training on Polish territory; strengthening partnership ties between Ukraine and the Nordic and Baltic countries in the field of security and defense. In summary, the General Staff stresses that the united efforts of the allies enable high-quality training of Ukrainian troops in Europe and strengthen defense cooperation with regional countries. It features: • 2 and 3-bedroom apartments • Amenities: swimming pool, fully equipped fitness center, club house, BBQ & gazebo terrace, children’s playground, and landscaped gardens Book Service Ad • Skyrise Apartments, Kampala 29s Skip Visit Sponsor A severe public health crisis has erupted on the outskirts of Damaturu, the Yobe State capital, where five residents of the Malam Matari community are currently hospitalized following a vicious attack by a rabid dog. The victims, who sustained deep lacerations and puncture wounds, are undergoing intense medical treatment, including the administration of life-saving post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) vaccines, to halt the progression of the universally fatal zoonotic disease. The Yobe State Government, under the directive of Governor Mai Mala Buni, immediately activated a veterinary rapid response team to contain the outbreak. The incident highlights the chronic vulnerability of semi-urban and rural Nigerian communities to zoonotic pathogens, driven by large populations of unvaccinated stray canines and a systemic lack of public awareness regarding immediate wound management protocols. The Incident in Malam Matari The attack occurred without warning, spreading panic through the densely populated Malam Matari community. The rabid dog engaged in highly aggressive, unprovoked behavior—a hallmark clinical sign of the furious form of rabies encephalitis—before being neutralized by local residents. Laboratory confirmation subsequently verified the presence of the lyssavirus. Veterinary Officer Dr. Yau Buba Wakil, who is leading the state’s sensitization and containment exercise, confirmed that the government has secured and distributed the necessary PEP vaccines. The rapid deployment of the vaccine is critical; once clinical symptoms of rabies—such as hydrophobia, hallucinations, and paralysis—manifest in a human patient, the mortality rate is 100 percent. The Damaturu Local Government, supported by Chief Sanitation Officer Ibrahim Aliyu, has launched a sweeping public health campaign to educate residents on identifying symptomatic animals and the urgent necessity of reporting bites. Global Health Protocols and Kenya Parallels The control of canine rabies is a massive challenge across Sub-Saharan Africa. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that rabies kills tens of thousands of people annually across the continent, with children under 15 accounting for 40 percent of fatalities. The global health body mandates that mass dog vaccination campaigns covering at least 70 percent of the canine population are the only proven method to break the transmission cycle to humans. In East Africa, Kenya’s Zoonotic Disease Unit (ZDU)—a collaborative agency between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture—has pioneered a highly effective strategic framework to eliminate human dog-mediated rabies by 2030. The Kenyan model relies on free, decentralized mass vaccination clinics and strictly enforced legislation under the Rabies Control Act, which holds pet owners criminally liable for failing to vaccinate domestic dogs. The integration of such strict legal frameworks presents a viable blueprint for Yobe State and the broader Nigerian federal health architecture. Critical Response Mechanisms Dr. Wakil’s veterinary rapid response team has outlined critical emergency protocols for the residents of Damaturu to prevent further infections. The public health directives include the following vital steps: Immediate Wound Management: Thoroughly washing any dog bite or scratch with soap and running water for a minimum of 15 minutes to physically flush the viral load from the tissue. Urgent Medical Intervention: Seeking immediate clinical care for the administration of the Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) and the multi-dose PEP vaccine schedule. Animal Observation: Quarantining the offending animal for 10 days, if safely possible, to observe for clinical signs of rabies. Community Reporting: Utilizing established hotlines to notify the veterinary response team of any stray dogs exhibiting hyper-salivation, unprovoked aggression, or erratic behavior. The Economic Burden of Zoonotic Outbreaks The financial cost of managing a rabies outbreak is staggering. The procurement of human PEP vaccines is notoriously expensive on the global pharmaceutical market, often costing upwards of $50 (KES 6,600) per dose, a price completely out of reach for the average rural Nigerian household. By subsidizing the treatment, the Yobe State government has averted a localized tragedy, but reliance on emergency procurement is fiscally unsustainable. International health experts warn that reactive treatment models must be replaced by proactive vaccination programs. Vaccinating a dog costs mere fractions of a dollar compared to treating a human victim. As urbanization encroaches on wild habitats across Northern Nigeria, the interface between humans and unvaccinated animal populations will only increase. Dr. Wakil urged residents to strictly adhere to the sensitization guidelines, noting that absolute community vigilance is the only permanent defense against the deadly virus. Book Service Ad • Novus Consult 28s Skip Visit Sponsor Health and agricultural authorities in Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory (FCT) have issued an urgent public health alert following a confirmed rabies outbreak that has claimed the lives of two residents. The fatalities, resulting from bites by infected stray dogs, have exposed critical vulnerabilities in the region’s animal vaccination protocols and triggered an immediate crisis response. Dr. Karnak Dandam, Director of Veterinary Services at the FCTA Agriculture and Rural Development Secretariat, confirmed the deaths occurred in the Gwagwalada and Kwali Area Councils. Laboratory analysis conducted by the National Veterinary Research Institute (NVRI) in Vom, Plateau State, verified the presence of the deadly Lyssavirus in eight recent cases across the two districts. The Anatomy of the Outbreak The confirmed cases, recorded between March and June 2026, indicate a sustained circulation of the virus within the local animal population. Of the eight confirmed infections, five originated in Gwagwalada, with the remaining three documented in Kwali. While the FCTA had initiated a vaccination campaign for dogs and cats across the territory in December 2025 and January 2026, Dr. Dandam acknowledged a significant systemic failure: the vaccine supplies were grossly insufficient to cover the target population. Consequently, a substantial reservoir of unvaccinated domestic and stray animals remained vulnerable, facilitating the current transmission chain. Rabies is an acute viral disease that almost exclusively targets the central nervous system. Transmitted via the saliva of an infected animal—typically through a bite or deep scratch—the disease is virtually 100 percent fatal once clinical symptoms emerge. Early human symptoms mirror flu-like conditions, including fever and fatigue, before rapidly progressing to neurological severe distress, hallucinations, and death. Emergency Protocols and Public Advisory In response to the fatalities, the FCTA is aggressively procuring additional vaccine doses to launch a comprehensive mass vaccination campaign targeting every canine and feline across all six area councils. Concurrently, authorities have issued strict directives to residents: Confinement: Pet owners must confine all vaccinated dogs and cats to prevent them from mingling with potentially infected stray populations. Immediate Action: Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal must immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water—a critical first-aid step that significantly reduces viral load—before seeking emergency post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) at a healthcare facility. Observation: Residents are urged to report any sudden behavioral changes in animals, such as unprovoked aggression, excessive salivation, or unusual isolation. A Broader African Public Health Challenge The lethal outbreak in Abuja highlights a persistent zoonotic threat across the African continent. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that rabies causes tens of thousands of deaths annually, predominantly in rural areas of Africa and Asia, with children under 15 being the most frequent victims. The logistical and financial hurdles of maintaining high vaccination coverage in animal populations are mirrored across East Africa. In Kenya, the Zoonotic Disease Unit (ZDU) has implemented a strategic plan aimed at eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. However, like Nigeria, Kenya struggles with managing expansive stray dog populations and ensuring consistent vaccine cold-chain logistics in remote counties. The cost of a human PEP course—often exceeding tens of thousands of Naira (thousands of KES)—remains prohibitively expensive for low-income families, reinforcing the absolute necessity of subsidizing mass animal vaccinations as the primary preventative measure. Securing the Capital’s Health Infrastructure The tragedy in the FCT underscores the critical importance of the "One Health" approach, which recognizes the deep interconnection between human health, animal health, and the environment. Failing to adequately fund veterinary services directly jeopardizes human lives. As the FCTA scrambles to deploy the newly procured vaccines, the success of the containment strategy will rely heavily on community compliance and the rapid mobilization of veterinary teams to eliminate the viral reservoir in the capital’s outskirts. news.content: nawaiwaqt group News Paper & TV Channel Roznama Nawaiwaqt Waqt News TV Magazines Sunday Magazine Family Magazine Nidai Millat Mahnama Phool Saturday, July 18, 2026 e-Paper Today's Paper EDITOR'S PICKS Newspaper Picks OPINION Editorials Columns Letters NEWS Latest Headlines Top Stories National Sports Lifestyle & Entertainment Business International Editor's Picks Snippets Lahore Karachi Islamabad MULTIMEDIA News In Pictures Cartoons Videos BLOGS Blogs Write for Us AI Use Policy CONNECT WITH US Get Alerts Health minister approves national rabies control framework Web Desk 2:39 PM | July 13, 2026 National Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ISLAMABAD: Federal Minister for National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination Mustafa Kamal on Monday voiced serious concern over the increasing number of rabies cases and dog bite incidents across Pakistan, calling for urgent nationwide measures to tackle the preventable yet deadly disease. The minister made the remarks during a meeting with a delegation from the Indus Hospital & Health Network (IHHN), led by its Chief Executive Officer Dr Abdul Bari Khan, to discuss a comprehensive national strategy for rabies prevention and control. During the meeting, the delegation briefed the minister on the country's rabies situation, highlighting the absence of an effective national rabies surveillance system. BISP payments suspended in Shangla due to biometric SIM shortage According to estimates shared during the briefing, around 5,000 people die from rabies each year in Pakistan, while hundreds of thousands of dog bite cases are reported annually. Children and residents of rural and underserved urban areas are among the most vulnerable. Expressing deep concern over the growing burden of the disease, Mustafa Kamal gave in-principle approval for the development of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework aimed at strengthening prevention, surveillance and response efforts across the country. He also announced the formation of a National Technical Working Advisory Group, which will lead the preparation of the framework and coordinate nationwide efforts to combat rabies. Residents demand effective action as stray dog population increases in Rawalpindi The health minister stressed the need for a nationwide public awareness campaign to educate citizens about rabies prevention, the importance of seeking immediate medical treatment after animal bites, and timely vaccination. During the meeting, Dr Abdul Bari Khan presented the minister with the "Sindh Official Guidelines for Prevention of Human Rabies (2024)," developed with the technical assistance of The Indus Hospital and Health Network. The meeting was held days after another rabies case was reported in Karachi. On July 10, a 28-year-old woman, identified as Malookan Bibi from Khwaja Ajmer Nagri in North Karachi, was admitted to the emergency department of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC) after developing symptoms of the fatal viral disease. analysis.brief_en: On 13 July 2026, Pakistan’s federal health minister approved a national rabies control framework and announced a technical advisory group to lead prevention and response efforts. The move follows concern over an estimated 5,000 annual rabies deaths and hundreds of thousands of dog bites nationwide. A recent Karachi case highlights ongoing transmission risks. The framework aims to strengthen surveillance, public awareness, and timely post-bite vaccination, while Sindh’s 2024 guidelines were presented as a model. Current gaps include the absence of a national surveillance system.

(Photo: AdobeStock)Comment on this story2CommentShare storySharetopics: RabiesTehama CountyBatsPet VaccinationsPublic HealthAnimal BitePost-Exposure TreatmentCalifornia Department of Fish and WildlifeRight arrowTEHAMA — Two bats found in residential areas of Tehama County recently tested positive for rabies, prompting county health officials to remind residents to avoid contact with wild animals and ensure pets are vaccinated.The Tehama County Health Services Agency said rabies is a fatal viral disease that affects the central nervous system and can spread to humans and other mammals through the bite of an infected animal. Health officials said the disease is preventable if people take proper precautions and seek treatment promptly after a potential exposure.Officials urged residents not to handle, feed or attempt to capture unfamiliar, stray or wild animals, including bats and feral cats. Pet owners are encouraged to keep animals on a leash during outdoor activities and prevent them from interacting with wildlife.Children also should be taught not to approach unfamiliar animals, even if they appear friendly, according to the agency.Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water and seek medical attention. Residents who believe they have been exposed to a potentially rabid animal should contact the Tehama County Health Services Agency Public Health Division at (530) 527-6824.Powered By 10 Sec Two Tehama County bats test positive for rabies; officials urge pet vaccines and caution NextStay Health officials also reminded pet owners to keep rabies vaccinations current through a licensed veterinarian.According to the agency, bats are the primary source of human rabies infections in the United States. While domestic animals account for fewer than 10% of reported rabies cases nationwide, rabies remains widespread among bats in Tehama County.Officials cautioned that rabid animals do not always display the commonly associated symptoms of excessive drooling or foaming at the mouth. Instead, infected animals may appear unusually aggressive or tame, stagger, become active during the day if they are normally nocturnal, or show other abnormal behavior.If left untreated, rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop. Early symptoms include fever, headache and fatigue before progressing to neurological symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations, difficulty swallowing and paralysis.Health officials said modern post-exposure treatment consists of four vaccine injections administered over two weeks, along with an injection of rabies immune globulin on the first day of treatment. The treatment is highly effective when started promptly after exposure.Residents who observe sick, injured or distressed wildlife are encouraged to report the animal to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. news.content_title: Rabies cases in RI are already outpacing recent years. What to know.
news.content: LOCAL Rabies cases in RI are already outpacing recent years. What to know. Thirty-two humans have been exposed to rabies and received treatment in Rhode Island this year Jack Perry Providence Journal July 16, 2026, 3:13 p.m. ET Keep Watching Rhode Island has seen a rise in rabies cases in 2026, surpassing the previous five-year average. State officials warn residents to avoid contact with wild animals to prevent exposure to the fatal disease. Raccoons and bats are the primary carriers of rabies identified in the state this year. An average of 24 animals in Rhode Island tested positive for rabies in each of the last five years, but 25 animals have already tested positive in 2026, with the year little more than half over. Thirty-two humans have been exposed to rabies and received treatment in Rhode Island this year, according to a joint press release from the Rhode Island Department of Health and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management. State officials took the opportunity on Thursday, July 16, to again remind Rhode Islanders about the importance of protecting themselves against the disease, which is fatal if not treated in time. Director of Health Dr. Jerry Larkin, said, “Being active in nature regularly is one of the best things you can do for your health. However, you should never touch a wild animal. "Any contact with a wild mammal puts you at risk for rabies.” Where have rabid animals been found? Rhode Island State Veterinarian Dr. Scott Marshall said, "Any direct contact with a wild mammal should be considered a potential rabies exposure." He said people should not approach or feed wild animals and should "report animals behaving unusually to authorities.” The majority of the rabid animals caught this year have been in the northern part of the state, according to state officials. Raccoons have accounted for the most, 14, followed by bats, 7. A rabid cat, coyote, skunk and a woodchuck have also tested positive this year, officials said. Rabies is most commonly transmitted through the bite of an infected animal, but it can also spread when saliva from a rabid animal enters the body through a scratch or an open wound, according to state officials. State law requires all dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies. State officials say vaccinating pets prevents them from getting rabies and prevents people from becoming exposed to rabies through their pets. The health department recommends the following additional steps to prevent rabies: Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. Protect your pets by always maintaining control; walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard; and do not let pets wander unsupervised. Securely cover all garbage cans so wild animals cannot scavenge for food. What to do if a person or pet comes into contact with a wild animal Anyone who has had direct contact with a wild mammal should immediately call RIDOH's Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology at 401-222-2577 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. or 401-276-8046 after hours). A RIDOH nurse will assess the exposure and determine whether post-exposure treatment is recommended. If needed, RIDOH will coordinate a post-exposure vaccine series. If any domestic animal, such as pets or livestock, had contact with a wild mammal, or if you are in possession of an animal that you suspect has rabies, call RIDOH, your local animal control officer, and your veterinarian. Daily briefs news Hancock County bat tests positive for rabies By SARA ARTHURS saraarthurs@thecourier.com saraarthurs@thecourier.com FINDLAY — Hancock Public Health reported Wednesday that a local bat has tested positive for rabies. Health Commissioner Lindsay Summit confirmed the bat was found in Hancock County, but declined to specify the location beyond that. “A family woke up to a noise and the bat was in the bedroom,” Summit said. The family brought the bat to the health department, which sent it to the Ohio Department of Health for testing, she said. They received the positive test results within 24 hours. Hancock Public Health then immediately contacted the family and encouraged them to contact their healthcare provider to see if they would need prophylactic treatment, Summit said. She said this is standard protocol. This is the first bat to test positive in Hancock County since 2009, Summit said. “This serves as an important reminder for everyone to take precautions to protect themselves and their families from exposure to bats,” stated the health department in a press release. Bats are the leading cause of rabies deaths for people in the United States. Every year, dozens of bats are submitted and test positive for rabies across the state of Ohio. Unfortunately, you cannot tell if a bat has rabies just by looking at it, and rabies can only be confirmed in a laboratory. If you have been in contact with a bat, even if you are not sure if you have been bitten or scratched, please contact the health department to discuss your rabies exposure risk and whether or not treatment is recommended. If you have any pets that may have been exposed to a bat, please consult your veterinarian for further instructions. The Ohio Department of Health notes that rabies from bats can spread to people even after seemingly minor bites or scratches. Summit added that, in some cases, people may not realize they have been bitten or scratched, so anyone who has had contact with a bat or found a bat in their home should reach out. “Err on the side of caution,” she said. Rabies causes encephalitis, a deadly neurologic disease, and is almost always fatal once symptoms develop, ODH states. Therefore, it is important to see if you might need treatment to prevent symptoms developing. “It is also important to vaccinate your pets against rabies, even if they are only indoor pets,” the ODH website states. “Bats can enter your home through an opening as small as a quarter inch to a half inch and can roost in areas of your home like attics, crawl spaces, and roofing. It is important to examine your home for holes that might allow bats to enter your living quarters.” Whenever possible, the bat should be captured and sent to a laboratory for rabies testing. Hancock Public Health can assist in this process of sending it for testing. “We’re talking about a disease with a 100% mortality rate,” said Dr. Tyler Fields, a veterinarian at Blanchard Valley Veterinary Clinic in Findlay. “It’s not really a disease we want to take a chance on.” Fields and his colleagues regularly hear from owners of indoor cats who decline to get them vaccinated against rabies, assuming they will never be exposed. But even a pet that never leaves the home might still be exposed if another animal gets in, he noted. People do report finding bats in their homes. “Accidents happen,” he said. Also, sometimes indoor cats escape and might roam the neighborhood for a few weeks. Once they come home, it’s hard to know what they might have been exposed to, Fields said. And there is no way to test a living animal for rabies. It can only be diagnosed postmortem, Fields said. Over time, he said, we have gotten better as a society at preventing rabies through vaccination – but this may mean we are further removed from rabies and may not be as aware of why it’s so vitally important to keep up the prevention. He added a professional concern is that the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recently paused its rabies testing program. News reports from April note that the CDC also paused testing for more than 20 other types of infectious disease. Fields encouraged owners to recognize the importance of prevention by getting their animals vaccinated. And, he said, please call your veterinarian if you have any questions. “We would rather have questions asked than something be assumed,” he said. Summit said that, even without a positive test, Hancock Public Health always assumes that diseases like rabies may be present in the community. She reminded residents to be cautious. For questions and concerns, contact Hancock Public Health at 419-424-7870. Comments (0) Comments are automatically disabled after 48 hours. news.content: Community Corner Rabies-Infected Bat Found At San Diego Zoo Safari Park The bat is the 19th to test positive for rabies this year in San Diego County. ESCONDIDO, CA — A wild bat found at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park tested positive for rabies, prompting county health officials to ask anyone who may have had contact with the animal to come forward. The deceased bat was found at 12:10 p.m. Saturday at the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant at the Escondido-based park. The animal was collected by a trained Safari Park employee. No human contact with the bat has been reported. The bat was not part of the park's animal collection. It was sent to the San Diego County Public Health Laboratory on Monday, where testing confirmed it had rabies. Find out what's happening in San Diegofor free with the latest updates from Patch. Anyone who touched the bat, or knows someone who may have, was urged to call County Public Health Services at 619-692-8499. Officials said only people who had direct contact with the animal are considered at risk. The bat is the 19th to test positive for rabies this year in the county. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive. Find out what's happening in San Diegofor free with the latest updates from Patch. "Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough," said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, the county's deputy public health officer. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies." Health officials reminded residents not to touch bats or other wildlife. Anyone who has direct contact with a bat should wash the area with soap and seek medical advice. Rabies symptoms can take weeks or months to appear, but treatment is highly effective when started before symptoms begin. Once symptoms develop, the disease is almost always fatal, officials said. Officials emphasized rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear, but treatment is highly effective if administered before symptoms develop. This is the 19th bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County in 2026.

news.content_title: Liverpool woman bitten by bat on holiday in Greece given life-saving rabies treatment
news.content: Liverpool woman bitten by bat on holiday in Greece given life-saving rabies treatment Laura Horton, from Mossley Hill, didn't realise the dangers when she picked up the bat in her hand Comments 5 News Holly Clarke TV Writer and Katie Pearson 11:37, 14 Jul 2026 Updated 11:37, 14 Jul 2026 View 3 Images The personal trainer from Mossley Hill was on a two-week birthday trip to Lesbos, Greece (Image: Laura Horton / SWNS) A woman from Liverpool was bitten by a bat on holiday in Greece. Laura Horton, 53, from Mossley Hill , requested advice for rabies treatment when she was on her two-week birthday trip to Lesbos in May. Article continues below Powered By 10 10 American recruits a 'couple of divvies' as he learns Scouse slang Share Next Stay The personal trainer shared her experience after she found a bat drowning in the swimming pool at the apartment complex where she was visiting a friend. Laura picked up the animal from the water and let it sit in her hand for 10 minutes to "dry off". She was unaware it had bitten her before flying away. ‌ It was AI tool "Google Lens" which warned Laura of the risks, and suggested she underwent treatment for rabies. ‌ The 53-year-old wanted to know what type of bat she had rescued, so she uploaded a photo of it sitting in the palm of her hand to Google Lens. As well as identifying it as a pipistrelle bat, it alerted her to seek medical treatment immediately due to the risk of contracting rabies from handling the animal. According to the NHS website, rabies is a rare but serious infection that is usually caught from an infected animal's bite or scratch, and it is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. View 3 Images She grabbed the animal from the water and let it sit in her hand for 10 minutes to "dry off" (Image: Laura Horton / SWNS) ‌ She claimed Google Lens warned her that she would be unable to feel a bat bite as their teeth are too small, and on closer inspection, Laura noticed two tiny pin-prick bite marks. Laura went to the Hospital of Mytilene, Lesbos , the following day, on May 8, where she started a course of preventative rabies post-exposure vaccines. She had a total of three jabs in Greece, followed by her fourth and final jab when she returned to the UK in June 1 at the School of Tropical Medicine, Liverpool. Article continues below Laura spoke to Talk to the Press about the experience. She said: "I had no idea you could catch rabies from a bat. I grabbed it from the water on instinct because it was drowning - I had no idea of the risks. "It sat on my hand for about 10 minutes, drying off. We all thought it looked cute, so I took a photo of it." After uploading the image to Google Lens to determine the species of bat, Laura was met with a series of questions from the AI tool. She said: "It started asking questions like, 'Are those your hands?' and 'Have you washed your hands for 15 minutes after handling it?' ‌ "It warned me of the risk of rabies and said I wouldn't feel a bite, as their teeth are too small. I thought it was all a bit dramatic. But when I took a photo of my hand, I saw two tiny bite marks." View 3 Images Laura Horton, 53, was bitten by the bat she rescued from the swimming pool (Image: Laura Horton / SWNS) Laura was four days into her two-week holiday in Petra in Lesbos, with friends when she was bitten. She rang her insurance company which confirmed she should seek medical attention. ‌ She needed to undergo a course of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) - a life-saving treatment given immediately after a potential bite or scratch from a rabid animal. Later that day, Laura went to the Lesbos hospital but claims a language barrier nearly prevented her from getting the correct treatment. She said: "At first, they tried to send me away with antibiotics. I'm not sure they understood what happened. I was sent to a travel clinic, and a nurse was furious I hadn't been given the first dose yet. I went back to the hospital and found the infectious diseases department - they were brilliant." ‌ She returned on May 11 and May 15 for two more jabs in Greece and had a fourth when she returned to the UK on June 1. She said: "My GP didn't actually know what to do. Luckily, we have the School of Tropical Medicine in Liverpool, and I was able to get my fourth injection arranged with them very easily. "I later found out there is a dedicated rabies hotline in the UK that would have delivered it to my doctor's surgery. It was lucky Google Lens told me to go to hospital - who knows what might have happened. "I read the tragic case about the boy in Canada who died after a bat landed on his face. A lot of people aren't aware of the dangers of these wild animals and the risks. Hopefully I can help raise awareness." Rabies is found throughout the world, but it's very rare in the UK. Rabies is spread by mammals, such as dogs, bats, raccoons and foxes. In the UK, it's only found in some bats. You should get medical attention immediately if: Article continues below you've been bitten or scratched by an animal while you're abroad. an animal has licked your eyes, nose or mouth, or licked a wound you have, while you're abroad. you've been bitten or scratched by a bat in the UK. If you're abroad, get medical help as soon as possible. Do not wait until you get back to the UK

analysis.brief_en: A 53-year-old woman from Liverpool, UK, was bitten by a bat while on holiday in Lesbos, Greece, in May 2026. Unaware of the bite, she sought medical advice after using an AI tool to identify the animal, which alerted her to the risk of rabies. She received a four-dose post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) course, with the first three doses administered in Greece and the final dose in Liverpool. Initial treatment was delayed due to a language barrier at the local hospital, but subsequent doses were completed without further issues. The incident highlights the risks of bat exposure and the importance of prompt medical attention.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 5 月,一名来自英国利物浦的 53 岁女性在希腊莱斯沃斯岛度假时被蝙蝠咬伤。她没有意识到自己被咬伤,在使用人工智能工具识别该动物后寻求医疗建议,该工具提醒她有狂犬病的风险。她接受了四剂暴露后预防(PEP)课程,前三剂在希腊注射,最后一剂在利物浦注射。由于当地医院的语言障碍,最初的治疗被推迟,但随后的剂量已经完成,没有出现进一步的问题。该事件凸显了接触蝙蝠的风险以及及时就医的重要性。

news.content_title: First Ottawa County rabies case of the year found in bat
news.content: HOLLAND TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WOOD) — The first Ottawa County animal case of rabies this year has been discovered after a bat tested positive for the disease Wednesday. The Ottawa County Department of Public Health did not specify where or when the bat was found, saying only it had been informed of the positive rabies test Wednesday. As of Monday, 21 cases of rabies have been found in bats across the state, with only one case of rabies being a skunk found in Oakland County, state data shows . No humans have contracted rabies in Michigan yet this year. The risk of exposure to rapid bats is higher from May through September when bats are most active. Health officials say to never touch or handle wild animals and urge people to vaccinate their pets against rabies. Exposure to rabies happens when people or pets are scratched or bitten by a rabid animal. Animals with rabies do not always appear sick and animals suspected of having rabies should be sent in for lab testing. If you believe you have found an animal that has rabies, contact the Ottawa County Department of Public Health or your local pest control. You can also bring an animal to the Harbor Humane Society for testing if you are able to catch it without making physical contact. If you suspect that you have been exposed to a rabid animal, even while asleep, you should seek treatment immediately, health officials say. Pets who have been exposed to a rabid animal should also receive veterinary care even if they are vaccinated against the disease. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. source on GoogleATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — A raccoon attacked by dogs in the Snellville area last week tested positive for rabies, according to Gwinnett County officials.Three dogs attacked the raccoon near Tree View Drive on Wednesday. As a precaution, the dogs are under evaluation and undergoing “rabies post-exposure management,” county officials said Monday.Rabies, a virus that attacks the central nervous system, is almost always deadly in humans if they don’t receive medical care before symptoms start. Early symptoms include fever, headache, weakness and discomfort.Residents should make sure their pets are up to date on their vaccines. Public health officials warn Snellville residents to stay away from animals behaving oddly, as the rabies virus is nearly always fatal if untreated. The three dogs involved are undergoing veterinary evaluations and strict rabies post-exposure management. SNELLVILLE, Ga. - A raccoon tested positive for rabies after a dog attack in Snellville, prompting public health officials to issue an immediate warning for residents to avoid animals behaving oddly. Rabid raccoon attack Related SearchesSearch for Budget Senior Monthly Phone Plan on Yahoo. View top results now.Yahoo | SponsoredSponsoredLearn more What we know: A raccoon tested positive for rabies after it was attacked by three dogs on July 8 near Tree View Drive in Snellville. The three dogs involved are currently undergoing veterinary evaluation and rabies post-exposure management, according to Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement and GNR Public Health. Officials advise all pet owners to make sure their pets are up to date on their rabies vaccinations. National Association of State Health Veterinarians guidelines state that unvaccinated dogs and cats exposed to a rabid animal must face a strict four-month quarantine and receive a vaccination one month before release. What is rabies? Dig deeper: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that the rabies virus attacks the central nervous system and is almost always fatal in humans if left untreated. Early symptoms in humans include a fever, headache and general weakness or discomfort. Health officials urge anyone bitten or scratched by a stray or suspected rabid animal to seek immediate medical care and report the exposure. Unusual animal behavior can be reported to the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office. Public health response What we don't know: Officials have not yet confirmed the current health status of the three dogs or whether they were vaccinated against rabies at the time of the confrontation. It remains unknown if any other wild animals or pets in the Snellville area were exposed to the rabid raccoon before the attack occurred. Protect your family What you can do: If you are bitten or scratched by a stray or suspected rabid animal, seek medical care immediately and tell your healthcare provider about the exposure. After seeking medical treatment, contact GNR Public Health at 770-339-4260 to speak with the on-call epidemiologist. To report an animal acting strangely and request a pickup, call the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office at 770-339-3200, ext. 5576. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement and GNR Public Health, who issued a joint public safety advisory, as well as medical data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and quarantine guidelines from the National Association of State Health Veterinarians. Raccoons Test Positive for Rabies in July; 8 Total this Season July 13, 2026 Sophia Peters, UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department has announced two more positive rabies cases found in raccoons this July, making the total number of positive cases eight this year. On Jul. 2, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Nithsdale on Caledonia Drive in Salisbury. Less than two weeks later, on Jul. 13, another raccoon tested positive for rabies; this time in the area of Archie Dennis Road in Parsonsburg after contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department continues to advise all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that another raccoon has tested positive for rabies, making it the fifth rabies case in Wicomico this year. On Friday, Jun. 12, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Kensington Woods and Upper Ferry Road in Salisbury Maryland, after contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. This update was published on Ju. 12 at 5:00 p.m. UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that another raccoon has tested positive for rabies, making it the fourth case in the county in just two months. On Tuesday, Apr. 28, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Hazel Street and Old Ocean City Road in Salisbury after having contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. This update was published on Apr. 28 at 3:28 p.m. WILLARDS, Md. – The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that a third raccoon in the county has tested positive for rabies. Officials say the raccoon was found near in the area of Rayne Road in Willards after it had contact with a dog. Two other rabid raccoons were located this month in Parsonsburg and Delmar. The WCHD is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with wild/stray animals. They also offer the following tips to protect your family and pets: Keep pets confined and avoid feeding them outside Teach children to leave unfamiliar animals alone Vaccinate pets Secure outside garbage bins Rabies is a preventable viral disease that exists in and is transmitted by the saliva of mammals. Maryland law requires all dogs, cats, and ferrets aged four months or older to have a current rabies vaccination. If left untreated, rabies is fatal. To report human or animal contact, such as bites or scratches, call WCHD at (410)-546-4446. news.content_title: Third Lane County bat tests positive for rabies, officials warn
news.content: A bat found in Lane County tested positive for rabies , and it's the third one so far this year, Lane County Public Health warned July 13. In the announcement, county and state officials urged members of the public to vaccinate their dogs and cats against rabies if they haven't already. "All pet owners should make certain their dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies. When our pets are protected from rabies, it provides a buffer zone of immune animals between humans and rabid wild animals, such as bats," said Dr. Emilio DeBess, state public health veterinarian. Thirteen bats have tested positive for rabies in Oregon so far this year. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of humans and mammals. It is "almost 100 percent" fatal once symptoms begin, the county said. The virus is carried in the saliva of an infected animal and can be transmitted when that animal bites, or in rarer instances, scratches another animal or person. If you or your pet is bitten by a bat, you should thoroughly clean the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention, report the event to Lane County Public Health and, if possible, capture the bat so it can be tested. There are several strains of rabies found in the U.S. but only bat rabies is found in Oregon. Other animals that have tested positive for rabies in Oregon contracted it from bats. According to Lane County, people should stay away from bats and not handle them. Alan Torres covers local government for the Register-Guard. He can be reached by email at atorres@registerguard.com , on X @alanfryetorres or on Reddit at u/AlfrytRG .
